title: How the Stage Was Set
framing: This prologue lists, in sourced steps, how oversight offices, ethics rules, the Justice Department and the clemency process changed around Trump before and during the acts this count records, and it closes with where the law stops at a sitting president, including what he backed and fought in Congress. It places those steps beside the acts without claiming that any step caused any act.
method: Seven themed finders read the Trump Tracker corpus (as of commit 32fa05b, with the seven setup entries and the stock-ban entry added on October 26, 2026) and the corruption ledger; a verifier per theme checked every beat against its entry (facts, verbatim sources, dates, quotes and who the entry attributes them to); a synthesis wrote the outline against the prior reviewed outline; a critic checked it against the reader’s four examples and for overreach; one gap-fill round followed. Every URL below appears in a tracker entry or the ledger; the gate ran after the sweep with zero misses.

sections.title: Removing the watchdogs
sections.thesis: After inspectors general examining two Cabinet members were removed in 2020, the second term removed 17 inspectors general, by a federal court's count, and the heads of the ethics and whistleblower-protection offices within weeks, removed an FEC commissioner before the commission lost its quorum, and won a ruling that the president may fire an FTC member without cause.

beats.line: In May 2020, Trump told Congress that State Department inspector general Steve Linick was out while Linick examined Pompeo's use of staff; the next day the acting Transportation inspector general, whose office was investigating Chao, was replaced.
beats.why: The ledger labels it obstruction of oversight and notes that successors later completed both investigations.

beats.line: In October 2020, Trump signed Executive Order 13957 creating Schedule F, which would have stripped job protections from tens of thousands of federal employees; Biden revoked it in January 2021.
beats.why: Trump vowed to reinstate it immediately if re-elected.

beats.line: On Friday evening, January 24, 2025, Trump fired 17 inspectors general by email, effective immediately, by a federal court's count, without the 30 days' notice to Congress the law requires.
beats.why: Removed agencies' independent fraud-and-waste investigators at once; a court found the notice law violated but declined to reinstate them, so the removals stood.
beats.quote: President Trump violated the IGA. That much is obvious.

beats.line: On February 7, 2025, a one-sentence White House email giving no reason fired Hampton Dellinger, head of the Office of Special Counsel, which protects federal whistleblowers; he sued, then dropped his case on March 6.
beats.why: The office that protects whistleblowers passed to acting heads, Doug Collins and then Jamieson Greer.
beats.quote: an independent watchdog and a safe, trustworthy place for whistleblowers to report wrongdoing and be protected from retaliation

beats.line: On February 10, 2025, three weeks into the term, Trump ousted David Huitema, the Senate-confirmed head of the Office of Government Ethics.
beats.why: The office certifies executive-branch financial disclosures and refused to certify Wilbur Ross's in the first term; the ledger files the removal under dismantling enforcement.

beats.why: Without a quorum the FEC cannot open investigations, fine violators or write rules; a complaint alleging Trump illegally controls MAGA Inc. cannot be decided.
beats.quote: the longest period without a quorum in the Commission's 50+ year history
beats.quoteBy: Shana M. Broussard, FEC chair, on the one-year anniversary of the lost quorum

beats.line: An OPM rule effective March 9, 2026 created Schedule Policy/Career, whose positions are at-will and excepted from adverse action appeals; it moved no one itself, and a June 3, 2026 executive order placed about 8,000 jobs in it, by the administration's count.
beats.why: Placed employees lose Merit Systems Protection Board appeals of adverse actions; whistleblower complaints go to their own agency, not the Office of Special Counsel. OPM says protections remain.

beats.line: On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Trump v. Slaughter that the president may fire an FTC member without cause, overruling the 1935 Humphrey's Executor precedent.
beats.why: The entry reads the logic as reaching the NLRB, Merit Systems Protection Board and Consumer Product Safety Commission; the Federal Reserve was excepted.

sections.title: Loosening the ethics rules
sections.thesis: Trump kept his businesses in a revocable trust under a company ethics plan with no ban on new foreign private deals, a first-day order revoked the appointee ethics pledge order, and later steps paused new foreign-bribery enforcement, ended ownership reporting for U.S. companies and withdrew the United States from Europe's anti-corruption monitor.

beats.line: The Trump Organization's second-term ethics plan put the businesses in a trust run by Trump's children and barred new deals with foreign governments but, unlike the 2017 plan, placed no ban on new foreign private deals.
beats.why: CNN noted the pledge was silent on how the company would handle overseas business deals.
beats.quote: The ethics pledge, however, is silent on how the company will handle overseas business deals
beats.quoteBy: CNN, on the plan

sources.text: CNN: Trump Organization's new ethics plan pledges Donald Trump will separate himself from his private business interests

beats.line: Trump took office in January 2025 without selling his assets or placing them in a qualified blind trust; they sit in a revocable trust overseen by Donald Trump Jr. that Trump can amend or revoke.
beats.why: Unlike a blind trust, it leaves him owning the businesses; the ledger records deals, token sales and licensing fees flowing to it.

beats.line: On January 20, 2025, Executive Order 14148 revoked Executive Order 13989, under which appointees had pledged to take no gifts from registered lobbyists and to observe two-year revolving-door limits.
beats.why: The ledger classes the revocation under dismantling enforcement.

beats.line: On February 10, 2025, Executive Order 14209 told the attorney general to cease new Foreign Corrupt Practices Act investigations or enforcement actions during a 180-day review.
beats.why: The ledger files the pause under dismantling enforcement; the order's title frames it as serving American economic and national security.

beats.line: On August 11, 2026, FinCEN issued a final rule permanently ending the requirement that U.S. companies report their beneficial owners, and said it will delete ownership information already filed by U.S. persons now exempt.
beats.why: The requirement was meant to make anonymous shell companies harder to use; deleting filed records means a later administration cannot simply restore them.
beats.quote: eliminating a burdensome reporting requirement for millions of law-abiding business owners without compromising our national security
beats.quoteBy: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent

beats.line: On September 28, 2026, the United States notified the Council of Europe that it is leaving GRECO, its anti-corruption monitoring group, which it joined in 2000; only Russia and Belarus have left before.
beats.why: The State Department framed the exit as ending payments to international bureaucracies; the Council of Europe says GRECO remains open to resuming cooperation.
beats.quote: The era of writing blank checks to international bureaucracies is over.
beats.quoteBy: The State Department

sections.title: The law's limits around a sitting president
sections.thesis: The Supreme Court held that a former president is absolutely immune from criminal prosecution for his core constitutional acts, at least presumptively immune for other official acts and not immune for unofficial ones; a judge dismissed one federal case against Trump and the special counsel then dropped both, citing the Justice Department's bar on prosecuting a sitting president; Trump backed a stock-trading ban limited to Congress and attacked the one bill that also covered the president; presidents are exempt from the conflict-of-interest law binding other executive employees; and the stablecoin law's bar on profiting did not extend to him.

beats.line: On July 1, 2024, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Trump v. United States that a former president has absolute immunity from criminal prosecution for acts within his conclusive and preclusive constitutional authority, at least presumptive immunity for other official acts, and none for unofficial acts.
beats.why: The ruling does not put a president beyond prosecution: unofficial acts get no immunity. It limits prosecution for official acts, and it did not decide whether a sitting president can be indicted; that bar is Justice Department policy, which the opinion notes in a footnote.
beats.quote: The President enjoys no immunity for his unofficial acts, and not everything the President does is official.
beats.quoteBy: Chief Justice John Roberts, for the majority

critic.verdict: The outline is close to complete and mostly faithful. All four of the reader's examples are covered: (1) inspectors-general-purge, printed as 17 by a federal court's count on January 24, 2025; (2) the stock-trading ban, where Trump's position is stated as the entry states it (he backed a Congress-only ban and attacked the one bill that covered the president), never as the reader framed it; (3) loyalists, across seven entries; (4) Blanche, his former personal criminal defense lawyer, as acting and then confirmed attorney general. Every setup act on the checklist is present, through a tracker entry or a ledger item. The OGE director's removal, the ethics-pledge revocation, the FCPA pause and the refusal to divest have only ledger items, and the first two are also stated in propublica-financial-conflicts-appointees. The most useful additions would be: blanche-ag-nomination-survivors-psa-nyc-bar-unfit, to give the fourth example its own beat; trump-would-pardon-administration-members-time-interview, which the gaps wave off but which is a setup act on its face; and, optionally, jan6-mass-pardons and the DOJ exodus entry. Three fixes should come before story mode is rebuilt: drop or attribute the limits thesis's unsourced 'lack enforcement absent Justice Department action' clause; rewrite the H.R. 7008 line to match the stock-ban entry (House GOP leaders inserted the voter-ID provision, and OMB endorsed the combined bill); and replace the Q1 beat's '3,700 trades' with the corrected count of about 3,640. The Schedule Policy/Career claims rest on a thin, un-updated entry. The revocable-trust 'precondition' why contradicts the framing's promise not to claim causation. The remaining items are wording-level tightenings.

readerNotes.intro: This screen sets out the prologue's limits as its checks found them: reasons resting on a reading rather than a finding, stand-in dates, shortened quotations and matters still alleged or unsettled. The full working notes follow below.

items.text: Trump backed a stock-trading ban limited to Congress and, on July 30, 2025, attacked Sen. Hawley after a committee advanced the one bill also covering the president. This page does not say he kept Congress from banning stock trading.

The bill he urged, H.R. 7008, excludes the president, and no source shows him pressing Republicans to weaken a Congress-only ban. Its failed Senate vote, 53-47 on September 30, 2026, is listed as a limit in the law.

Seven steps give reasons drawn by inference, not stated in their records: Kash Patel's appointment, Pam Bondi's confirmation, her firing, the ethics-pledge revocation, the foreign-bribery enforcement pause, the first-term clemency market and Liz Oyer's firing.

Ten other reasons carry a record's own analysis or label, not a finding: on Linick, the FTC ruling, the privilege opinion, Rogoff, the revocable trust, ownership reporting, pardon brokers, Trump's pardon remarks, Bloomberg's trade count and Schedule Policy/Career.
No section summary is marked as going beyond what its records state.

The summary for the section on removing watchdogs says an FEC commissioner was removed before the commission lost its quorum; the record says the quorum went as Republican commissioners left, so the summary gives order only.
The summary for the section on the law's limits sets Trump's own position on the stock-trading ban beside limits in the law.

Four dates stand in for others: Kash Patel's appointment, which has no date in its record; the 2020 Schedule F order, known only as October 2020; Todd Blanche's undated nomination; and his campaign step, dated by its record.

Other dates fall on a related event: the FEC quorum loss, Ed Martin's first post, Bondi's confirmation, news reports on the anti-corruption squad, the working group and first-term pardons, a record date for Oyer's firing, the Hawley vote, Bloomberg's analysis.

Several quotations are fragments, begin mid-sentence or omit the closing period: those from Dellinger, Trump on Hawley, Bessent, Bondi's memo, Sen. Warner, the FEC chair, Executive Order 14209, CNN, Van Hollen and Murray, and Eric Trump.
Judge Brann's quotation starts mid-sentence and keeps his lead-in, 'the Government tells us', so it is his account of the government's position, not a finding.

Some matters are allegations or one side's account: the MAGA Inc. complaint before the FEC, CREW's claim that the Bondi donation was a bribe, with no finding reported, Oyer's account of her firing, and the pardon brokers' own claims.

No pardon in exchange for payment is established. The end of the FBI bribery investigation is ProPublica's reporting, and no source shows a motive to shield anyone. 'Enemies list' is CNN's label; Patel denies it is one.

Some steps are not final: the state bar rule is a proposal, and its conflict with the McDade Amendment is its opponents' view; the Rogoff and OPM-question rulings are preliminary; the Halligan dismissals were without prejudice.
No source shows Trump influenced the Cannon ruling, and the elector-slate pardon proclamation's legal effect is mostly symbolic.

Five phrases were checked in an earlier version, not the latest: Bondi's 'failure to prosecute his political enemies', the privilege opinion's 'first time', the department's word that ethics approved Blanche's convention appearance, other agencies' cuts, and the range-based disclosures reason.
The count of 17 inspectors general removed in January 2025 is a federal court's; another record, on the Social Security inspector general, gives 19, which is not used.
The step on Eric Trump's blind-trust claim prints 'more than 3,600 trades'; the record's correction gives about 3,640, made up of 2,345 purchases and 1,296 sales.
One source for the step on the privilege opinion, from PBS, cannot be checked automatically; it is not that step's only source.
The 'severe' rating on the step on the September 30 Senate vote is the rating of the SAVE America Act as a whole, not of the vote.
The step on the Supreme Court's July 1, 2024 immunity ruling was added last, drafted from its record alone and checked once.

The prologue leaves out matters outside its subject, which is the changes around the acts this count records, and acts the count records itself, such as the NLRB and EAC quorum losses, tariffs, the Qatar jet and individual pardons.

First-term ethics matters, among them the GSA hotel lease, foreign-profit payments, Wilbur Ross's divestiture, 2020 Hatch Act violations and Jared Kushner's clearance, are not included; the reasons offered for the Ross and Kushner matters did not pass checking.
